newsitem.title: TURKEY: Iraq's Saddam now has Kurdish card against Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Saddam now has Kurdish card against Turkey.

text.p: Saddam Hussein's return to northern Iraq has handed him a potential new weapon against neighbouring Turkey -- the separatist rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) who are fighting for autonomy from Ankara.

With Baghdad's influence now extending all the way to its northern border, the Iraqi president can pressure Turkey by unleashing PKK fighters based in camps along the Iraqi frontier, domestic analysts and foreign diplomats say.

At the same time, they say, Baghdad's new Kurdish allies, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), have filled a five-year vacuum and limited Turkey's ability to project military force and political influence into northern Iraq.

"The fact is the PKK will go on existing and being effective in the region. Now, all depends on Baghdad's directives," political scientist Dogu Ergil told Reuters on Monday. "Will Saddam now use the PKK card against Turkey?"
A Western diplomat with extensive experience in the north said: "We can now expect the Turks to have a much tougher time."
Already, more than 20,000 people have died in the PKK's guerrilla war, which has tied up more than 250,000 troops in eastern Turkey at an estimated annual cost of $8 billion.

Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller this month announced ambitious plans for a "security cordon" up to 10 km (six miles) deep inside Iraq to choke off PKK infiltration. The army, accustomed to regular security sweeps across the border, vowed to "go in and stay in."

Two weeks on, military planners are talking about stationing electronic monitoring devices, not troops, while the foreign ministry is smarting from Arab and western protests in defence of Iraqi territorial integrity.
"There are new facts in the north of Iraq. That area is no longer free for all," Iraqi presidential adviser Hamed Youssef Hummadi warned the Turks last week.

Even Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Sabah of Kuwait, Iraq's staunchest regional foe, blasted the Turkish plan at a weekend meeting of Arab ministers: "We are the people most committed to the coherence of Iraq...We cannot accept the partition of Iraq."
Nor can Ankara expect KDP warlord Massoud Barzani -- now, with Saddam's backing, master of the north -- to take on the PKK in exchange for aid and political support as he once did.
"There is cetainly no cooperation between us and the PKK against Turkey," Barzani told Cumhuriyet daily.
"But we would not fight against a Kurdish organisation such as the PKK for Turkey's sake. As long as it does not pose problems for (Iraqi) Kurdistan, it can stay there."
KDP peshmerga leaders inside Iraq said they had no plans to move against PKK positions, clustered not far from the main Iraqi border town of Zakho that is now under KDP control.
"We do not have any orders to move against the PKK, and we do not expect to receive such orders," one KDP official told Reuters.

Deprived of influence on the ground, Turkey appears about to lose its last window on PKK activities -- the U.S.-led air umbrella that has sheltered Kurds of the north from Iraqi forces since a failed uprising after the 1991 Gulf War.
Pressure is mounting in Turkey to deprive that mission, Operation Provide Comfort (OPC), of its Turkish base to end what domestic critics term a surrender of Turkish sovereignty.
Ending surveillance by U.S., British, French and Turkish planes would deprive Ankara of valuable intelligence on the PKK and the political "cover" for periodic bombing of rebel targets in Iraq.

"The fate of the PKK lies in the hands of Barzani and Saddam, as well as Turkey. It now depends on whether Saddam and Barzani give any guarantees to Turkey," said political commentator Mehmet Ali Birand.
"Of course, Turkey will have to give things in return -- lifing OPC and forget the security cordon. It is a give-and-take business," he told Reuters.
